So back to the question- how should we describe scholarly infrastructure that is affordable to all and where the costs associated with participating in and running it are distributed fairly? Maybe we need to use the word "equitable" in addition to "open?" 

"POESI?"
Cynics would claim that the "stakeholders" are the people who pay. But again, in POSI, we explicitly reject that view.  https://t.co/pNWJiNY4bp

There is also question-begging when we talk about infrastructure cost from the opposite perspective- with phrases like "community funded/subsidized." Who in the community is subsidizing it? Or which stakeholders?
In POSI, we use the term "stakeholder." Parties can have a stake in an infrastructure running but may not be direct users/customers of it.
I also worry about focusing on the "user" because that word starts quickly becoming conflated with "customer" and the unhelpful baggage that brings to the conversation.
This is partly why it is easy to underfund infrastructure- so many people don't realize the second-order benefits of the system.

Besides, with infrastructure, I think there is a danger in tying its value too directly to "users." A fundamental characteristic of infrastructure is that there are parties who benefit from its existence but who may not be direct users of the system.

Free-to-use" or "free-at-point-of-use" raises the question- "use by whom?" In DataCite/Crossref, is the party resolving the DOI or using our APIs "the user?" (they don't pay). Or is the party registering the DOI "the user?" (they do pay). Same with “price-free.” Somebody pays.

"Subsidized," "free to use,"  and "community-funded" are all vast improvements over "cost-free," for describing open scholarly infrastructure. but I wonder if we need to get the word "equitable" in there? https://t.co/BfqlKY7SQ8
@MikeTaylor @kodertj In POSI we use the term "stakeholder." There are parties who have a stake in an infrastructure running but who may not be direct users/customers of it.
@MikeTaylor @kodertj I suspect that this assumption that infrastructure users are synonymous with "customers" is the root of the problem of trying to get scholarly infrastructure adequately funded.

@MikeTaylor @kodertj Besides, with infrastructure, I don't think the term "user" is useful as it starts quickly becoming conflated with "customer" and all the unhelpful baggage that brings to the conversation.

@MikeTaylor @kodertj Who is "the user?" The answer differs with each infrastructure. Even within one infrastructure, there may be different kinds of users. In DataCite/Crossref, is the person resolving the DOI the user, or is the party registering the DOI the user? Or both?
Disclosure: I work for @CrossrefOrg. I am also a co-author of The Principles for Open Scholarly Infrastructure. And I am cranky. Bad takes are my own.

And if I were a potential user of said service, I'd be wondering what happens after those four years of funding run out.
</rant>
And frankly, if I were a funder, I'd be a little bemused at seeing the phrase "cost-free" in a presentation talking about a service I'd just funded for four years.
But in *any* scenario, using the phrases "no-cost" and "cost-free" is damaging the cause of getting funders to take open scholarly infrastructure seriously.
Or perhaps they conflate "no direct charge to the end-user" with "no-cost?" If so, they might want to speak with their accounting department.
And even in this charitable interpretation, the subtext is "the cost is not outsourced to parties we disapprove of."
Frankly, the most charitable interpretation of "cost-free" open infrastructure I can think of is that they mean the cost is not outsourced.

The idea that "open scholarly infrastructure" can be "cost-free" epitomizes the contempt that some (not all!) researchers have for the labor of the supporters that keep their institutions running and who make their research possible.
But I digress.
Or that throwing the "distributed" magic pixie dust at the infrastructure problem solves anything at all.
As they should by implying that throwing the "distributed" magic pixie dust at the infrastructure problem somehow makes the costs vanish.

And people who know better but who still use the rhetorical device of trying to reduce an entire infrastructure and the people running it to the comparative triviality of simply "minting identifiers" should be ashamed of themselves.
(Unless, apparently, they are graduate students or postdocs and you think borderline poverty + no work/life balance is “cost-free”)
People working late into the night and over weekends and holidays to answer questions and keep APIs working are not "cost-free."

At the very least, implying that *any part* of open scholarly infrastructure can be "cost-free" is an erasure of the many people responsible for keeping machines running, answering questions, and managing services.
<rant>People who use the phrases "no-cost" or "cost-free" when talking about open infrastructure (scholarly or otherwise) are being either naïve or disingenuous.

@MikeTaylor Cool. Thanks. I had planned a blog post. You just poked me at the right time. I will redraft as one.

@keith_wilson Except that the fragility of an identifier correlates strongly with the degree to which semantic information is embedded in it (remember SICIs?). So generally preferable to put version information in the metadata and make the identifier itself opaque.
NB that the software comparison breaks down in some cases, - particularly around the phrase "breaking changes"- but that is a subject for another day.
It is this latter thing that DOIs do when they are used in a citation context (e.g. by @CrossRefOrg, @DataCite, etc.).

Minor copyediting changes should be treated similarly. They might result in a different hash, but you still want something other than the hash that tells you whether the change was likely to have effected the meaning.

And the same is true with content. The bytestream of the PDF and HTML copies of an article will be different, but not in a way that would normally effect crediting/interpretation of the work and so we don't assign separate citation identifiers to them.

On the other hand, the version number in software conveys changes that are considered more significant- those that might effect the performance characteristics or fix bugs (minor point releases) and those that break backwards compatibility (major point releases).

The hash alone can convey a change in the bytestream, but that change might be trivial and not merit even a minor version bump. For example, removing a blank line or automatically running your code through autopep8 when you save it.
Changes in the bytestream of something do not always correspond to changes in the "meaning."  This is why, even with software version control, we use both hashes and separate version numbers.

But if the single change is trivial, then having different DOIs for the two versions just muddies the citation record- because it (amongst many other things) makes it more difficult to detect when people have cited the same content.

This practice helps clarify the citation record. For example, it enables me in the future to easily detect when somebody cited the article with the wrong number vs the article with the corrected number.

@MikeTaylor @CrossrefOrg @qeios As I said- it *might* be important to assign a new DOI to a version that corrects a single character typo- If the correction changes the meaning or crediting of the work (e.g. adding a critical decimal point) (thread)
@MikeTaylor @CrossrefOrg @qeios “significant” means likely to change interpretation or crediting. Afraid that at some level it is an editorial decision and cannot always be decided automatically.

@MikeTaylor @CrossrefOrg @qeios Do not recommend assigning DOI to “most recent version” as that will change over time- so  seems dubious to “cite” something you haven’t seen yet. Instead you can use relations in metadata to point to more recent versions.
@MikeTaylor @CrossrefOrg @qeios Only recommend assigning DOIs if the difference between versions is significant.

@MikeTaylor @CrossrefOrg @qeios Guidance is that we use DOIs as citation identifiers. So different DOIs only for versions where change is likely to effect interpretation or crediting of the work. This is essentially an editorial decision.(e.g. A missing period may be trivial, unless it is a decimal point.)

@csarven @natesjacobs @lesliekwchan @ewout Again- for better or for worse, juridical entities live longer than people. Can therefor rent domains for longer. And make provisions for passing them on., etc.
@natesjacobs @csarven @lesliekwchan @ewout @sciteai @CrossrefOrg (50/50) Sorry about length. Hope that helps.
@natesjacobs @csarven @lesliekwchan @ewout @sciteai @CrossrefOrg (49/N) And promoting imperfect, centralised systems (Crossref, DataCite, ORCID) that, nonetheless, many find extremely useful.
@natesjacobs @csarven @lesliekwchan @ewout @sciteai @CrossrefOrg (48/N) And continue plugging governance over technology.

@natesjacobs @csarven @lesliekwchan @ewout @sciteai @CrossrefOrg (47/N) But, until somebody can propose a way to avoid the "distributed begets centralised" paradox, I will just give another resigned “sigh.”
@natesjacobs @csarven @lesliekwchan @ewout @sciteai @CrossrefOrg (46/N) Powered by bollocks-chain. Or LOD.
@natesjacobs @csarven @lesliekwchan @ewout @sciteai @CrossrefOrg (45/N) "Distributed open enterprise digital rights management fabric".
@natesjacobs @csarven @lesliekwchan @ewout @sciteai @CrossrefOrg (44/N) You can sprinkle it in with other technical terms to make a vague or daft idea sound plausible. Try it:

@natesjacobs @csarven @lesliekwchan @ewout @sciteai @CrossrefOrg (43/N) The word "distributed" has joined terms like "enterprise", "open", "framework", "fabric", "lightweight" and "agile" as technical magic pixie dust.
@natesjacobs @csarven @lesliekwchan @ewout @sciteai @CrossrefOrg (42/N) So... in summary my take is this...
@natesjacobs @csarven @lesliekwchan @ewout @sciteai @CrossrefOrg (41/N) Maybe there is hope.
@natesjacobs @csarven @lesliekwchan @ewout @sciteai @CrossrefOrg (40/N) But there are interesting efforts to get funders to think differently about scholarly infrastructure. https://t.co/gWku1P22m4
@natesjacobs @csarven @lesliekwchan @ewout @sciteai @CrossrefOrg (39/N) Where uptake will be unevenly distributed and hard to account for. Not ideal.

@natesjacobs @csarven @lesliekwchan @ewout @sciteai @CrossrefOrg (38/N) As long as funders keep pretending they are not funding scholarly infrastructure, the costs of identifiers, archiving, etc. will be collected further downstream.
@natesjacobs @csarven @lesliekwchan @ewout @sciteai @CrossrefOrg (37/N) Again, not perfect. But this may have more to do with the point where costs are recouped than with the costs themselves.

@natesjacobs @csarven @lesliekwchan @ewout @sciteai @CrossrefOrg (36/N) And we also want to encourage new developments in scholarly comms. Which is why we have different charges for different kinds of content types (preprints, data, software, etc).

@natesjacobs @csarven @lesliekwchan @ewout @sciteai @CrossrefOrg (35/N) And we are well-aware of the regressive nature of our fees. So we work with groups like Scielo, and INASP to reduce the costs and burdens of membership
@natesjacobs @csarven @lesliekwchan @ewout @sciteai @CrossrefOrg (34/N) Which brings us back to cost. It verges on obtuse to deny that there are costs to running these systems.
@natesjacobs @csarven @lesliekwchan @ewout @sciteai @CrossrefOrg (33/N) It might not be perfect (qv individual membership) but at least it a start.
@natesjacobs @csarven @lesliekwchan @ewout @sciteai @CrossrefOrg (32/N) Crossref, DataCite and ORCID are membership organisations. If you join them, you become part of their governance.
@natesjacobs @csarven @lesliekwchan @ewout @sciteai @CrossrefOrg (31/N) (More on governance of scholarly infrastructure here: https://t.co/VIuMLackDm )

@natesjacobs @csarven @lesliekwchan @ewout @sciteai @CrossrefOrg (30/N) Then it seems a good strategy would be to make sure that the governance of the centralised entity is controlled by the community it serves.
@natesjacobs @csarven @lesliekwchan @ewout @sciteai @CrossrefOrg (29/N) Fair enough.

@natesjacobs @csarven @lesliekwchan @ewout @sciteai @CrossrefOrg (28/N) You'd think we'd learn that perhaps the real issue is governance. Our worry about centralisation is shorthand for "we don't trust the centralised system will work in our interests."

@natesjacobs @csarven @lesliekwchan @ewout @sciteai @CrossrefOrg (27/N) Which brings us to "oligopoly", "monopoly", etc. Given the repeated pattern we have seen of distributed systems being co opted by centralised systems...

@natesjacobs @csarven @lesliekwchan @ewout @sciteai @CrossrefOrg (26/N) “Distributed begets centralised.” For every distributed communication system we have developed, somebody has had to develop a centralised system to make it usable.
@natesjacobs @csarven @lesliekwchan @ewout @sciteai @CrossrefOrg (25/N) And as soon as somebody offers deluxe, hosted, managed websites (or pods, or whatever), they will dominate the system.

@natesjacobs @csarven @lesliekwchan @ewout @sciteai @CrossrefOrg (24/N) Maintaining your own website (or "pod", or whatever) is a big time commitment. And only makes sense if you don't count your time as cost.
@natesjacobs @csarven @lesliekwchan @ewout @sciteai @CrossrefOrg (23/N) "Distributing" may hide the cost, but it also probably increases it.
@natesjacobs @csarven @lesliekwchan @ewout @sciteai @CrossrefOrg (22/N) (I didn't say I liked it- just that it jibes with reality.)
@natesjacobs @csarven @lesliekwchan @ewout @sciteai @CrossrefOrg (21/N) There may be few things I subscribe to in classical economics but "economies of scale" is one of them.
@natesjacobs @csarven @lesliekwchan @ewout @sciteai @CrossrefOrg (20/N) And the idea that somehow it would be cheaper (or free) if it were "distributed" seems fanciful.
@natesjacobs @csarven @lesliekwchan @ewout @sciteai @CrossrefOrg (19/N) And that costs money. And so does the technical stuff.

@natesjacobs @csarven @lesliekwchan @ewout @sciteai @CrossrefOrg (18/N) ... getting the membership to define & agree on their mutual obligations. And educating them. And then nagging them relentlessly.

@natesjacobs @csarven @lesliekwchan @ewout @sciteai @CrossrefOrg (17/N) We have joked that Crossref DOIs are only as persistent as Crossref staff. As a membership organization, most of our work is social...

@natesjacobs @csarven @lesliekwchan @ewout @sciteai @CrossrefOrg (16/N) But while we are on the subject of obligations... It is by now a truism that persistence is more a social problem than a technical one.
@natesjacobs @csarven @lesliekwchan @ewout @sciteai @CrossrefOrg (15/N) And we also have orgs that are made up of just one person (hint).
@natesjacobs @csarven @lesliekwchan @ewout @sciteai @CrossrefOrg (14/N) And we also have orgs that are just crap at meeting their responsibilities.

@natesjacobs @csarven @lesliekwchan @ewout @sciteai @CrossrefOrg (13/N) Clearly, identifier-dweebs are outliers in this case and would probably be more responsible than most orgs in meeting CR obligations.

@natesjacobs @csarven @lesliekwchan @ewout @sciteai @CrossrefOrg (12/N) So we have focused on orgs because they are generally better equipped to take on the responsibilities associated with updating their pointers (DOIs) and metadata.

@natesjacobs @csarven @lesliekwchan @ewout @sciteai @CrossrefOrg (11/N) They also, legally, tend to have well-documented provisions for maintaining & transferring assets (e.g. domains, content, etc). People, alas, don't.
@natesjacobs @csarven @lesliekwchan @ewout @sciteai @CrossrefOrg (10/N) But, for better or for worse, juridical persons (i.e. organizations) *can* have a much longer lifespan than actual people.

@natesjacobs @csarven @lesliekwchan @ewout @sciteai @CrossrefOrg (9/N) Which brings us to the issue of individual membership to orgs like DataCite and Crossref. Both orgs would love to enable individual membership.

@natesjacobs @csarven @lesliekwchan @ewout @sciteai @CrossrefOrg (8/N) It is inevitable that someday “https://t.co/EuIzphG0SB” will "belong" to somebody else. Using it as the foundation of a persistent identifier for my content would be folly.
@natesjacobs @csarven @lesliekwchan @ewout @sciteai @CrossrefOrg (7/N) There are myriad ways in which I could lose control of "https://t.co/EuIzphG0SB"- poverty, forgetfulness, divorce, death.

@natesjacobs @csarven @lesliekwchan @ewout @sciteai @CrossrefOrg (6/N) (FTR- I think use of the term "ownership" in the context of identifiers -personal or otherwise- is anathema. But that is another rant.)
@natesjacobs @csarven @lesliekwchan @ewout @sciteai @CrossrefOrg (5/N) This is an important characteristic because we *rent* domains, we don't "own" them.
@natesjacobs @csarven @lesliekwchan @ewout @sciteai @CrossrefOrg (4/N) A URI that points directly to a domain that has expired or changed hands cannot be re-pointed in this way.

@natesjacobs @csarven @lesliekwchan @ewout @sciteai @CrossrefOrg (3/N) But the indirection of pointers makes PIDs more "persistable" (a term I favour over “persistent”). Yes, a DOI might break, but it can be fixed by re-pointing it.

@natesjacobs @csarven @lesliekwchan @ewout @sciteai @CrossrefOrg (2/N) Plain URIs as PIDs pose problems when content moves between domains. Redirectable URIs (e.g. DOIs, Handles, ARKs) are just pointers.
